title: Graham Scott: Which referees impressed and disappointed me in 2025-26? And which laws must change?
content:
Premier League referees have had another tough season but the unpopular truth is that the standard is nothing like as bad as social media would have you believe.

Just like any other, the season has been sprinkled with shockers on the field and howlers in the VAR chair, but most of the confected rage is driven by still frames and slow-motion clips of decisions that could have gone either way or were definitively correct.

Fans are convinced that the officials in whichever league they follow are the worst on the planet, or that there is a conspiracy against their club. It makes me wonder why they are still paying to watch if they think everything’s fixed.

My positive spin should not mask the reality that I know there is work to do, mostly in relation to the on-field decision-making process. All media – professional and social – has become obsessed with VAR, but the issues that most urgently need addressing are on the pitch.

An assumption has taken hold that referees have stopped making decisions and become reliant on the safety net of VAR. Based on my own experience and knowing the 20 officials involved well, I remain to be convinced.

There is an element of truth to the assertion, because referees would much rather upgrade a caution to a dismissal than the reverse. It’s not ideal to award a penalty and then find yourself dropping the ball to the goalkeeper, or to send off a player only to wave them back on, but examples of referees ‘bottling it’ are rare.

There is little doubt, however, that corners have become a free-for-all and tackles that would have resulted in red cards five years ago are now routinely downgraded to yellows.

The referees and assistants meet weekly and discuss all the major talking points from the previous match round. The conversation is influenced heavily by the views of ex-players expressed anonymously through the Premier League’s key match incident (KMI) panel.

Its findings are not particularly meaningful, as some of its adjudications are mystifying in both directions, but it’s the only data there is. As of match day 36, refs had got 86 per cent of decisions correct, which is down from 87.2 per cent across the whole of 2024-25 but up slightly on the previous year. VAR errors are up from 18 to 23 at the same stage of last season, almost all for failing to intervene.

Behind the figures lies a more nuanced story. Over the past few seasons, the panel has endorsed referees’ calls that make corners look like scrummages – which, in turn, makes them impossible to police – and dangerous tackles that are excused for nebulous reasons, such as ‘lacking intensity’ or insufficient contact.

Like fans, I am weary of the tiresome farce that corners, long throws and other set pieces have become. The Premier League promised action and told referees to crack down – the third such initiative in 10 seasons.

But the KMI panel, appointed by the league to tell referees what constitutes an acceptable level of contact, proved predictably flaky. In week two it only endorsed a judo throw at Craven Cottage by a 3-2 margin, and in the third round voted 5-0 that a ref should have penalised a rugby tackle and 3-2 that the error was not ‘clear and obvious’.

Thereafter, only two more spot kicks were awarded by referees for holding at corners and the like, and another pair after a VAR intervention. The KMI panel reckoned four were missed by VARs all season.

It’s a similar story with red card tackles. With two weeks of the season to play, the KMI panel had assessed 45 challenges that were considered potential serious foul play. Of the nine judged incorrectly by the referee, only six were so clearly wrong that the VAR was expected to intervene. Interestingly, no one was sent off only to be recalled.

By contrast, three players were sent off and missed nine matches between them for briefly coming into contact with an opponent’s hair. I am yet to meet anyone in the game who thinks that makes sense, especially given what is allowed to pass.

The Premier League and chief refereeing officer Howard Webb will have a choice over the summer to take a tougher stance on holding and serious foul play, or risk even greater disillusionment with the product. Stand by for another August press call promising action.

One other point. Everyone in the game seems united that the handball law has become cumbersome, with its pick ‘n mix of considerations and mitigations, that even referees are receiving some sympathy.

FIFA says it wants to see a more consistent approach worldwide, so let’s hope that the Premier League’s view that handball should be penalised sparingly prevails. My hopes are not high, and the league has often ignored the game’s global governors anyway, but let’s see how the World Cup is officiated.

This is dangerous territory, because whoever I name will invite derision from a disgruntled fanbase somewhere. But anyway, here goes.

Peter Bankes earned the EFL Cup final with a string of impressive performances in the first two thirds of the season, so it’s a pity he was then injured for the run-in. He was tough on poor player behaviour, only made one mistake in relation to a key match incident before Christmas, and delivered the goods at Wembley.

Michael Oliver and Anthony Taylor both seem to be hitting the World Cup in good shape and have every chance of going deep in the tournament, especially if England are knocked out early.

Sometimes refs suffer from a combination of poor form and ill fortune, and Rob Jones seems to have been a victim of both.

Nothing seemed to go right after he was let down badly by a misguided – OK, indefensible – VAR intervention in his second match of the season, which led to him wrongly ruling out a Josh King goal for Fulham at Chelsea.

He missed a clear handball later in the game, five second yellow cards over the course of the season and latterly incorrectly awarded two penalties that are hard to explain.

Despite this critique, Jones has proved he’s good enough to thrive again with a good start to next season.

I liked FA Cup final referee Darren England’s decision to turn down a penalty appeal from Erling Haaland in his side’s home game with Nottingham Forest.

Having fallen for such a move myself, it was good to see a referee refuse to reward a player who kicks the ball past the advancing goalkeeper, then runs into his sprawling opponent and goes to ground.

Despite being further from the incident than ideal, England still made the right call and hopefully discouraged other strikers from trying the same trick.

England was the referee again here, but the bigger villain was the VAR in the Crystal Palace v Chelsea match.

The decision after review to award a penalty against Palace defender Jaydee Canvot for accidental handball on the goal line was plain wrong in law. Fortunately, it mattered little in the grand scheme of things (Chelsea won the game 3-1).

Jeremy Doku (Manchester City). Unlike so many of his contemporaries, Doku always looks to take on defenders rather than passing the buck, attacks with gusto and is more likely than most to stay on his feet in the tackle. Of course, he appeals for free kicks and penalties, but I have not seen him do so unreasonably and I am yet to see him dive.

James Garner (Everton). Nothing personal, I promise, but simply based on his record of 115 tackles and 12 yellow cards, both the highest in the league. I admire the energy and competitive spirit, but that looks too much like hard work.

Coventry City at home on the opening day next season. My first three matches refereeing them were at three different grounds, as they became a wandering team plummeting through the divisions. Their fans were always, understandably, miserable. It would be good to return in a more positive atmosphere.

The new rule requiring goalkeepers to release the ball in eight seconds or risk conceding a corner has been applied fairly and had a positive impact. I was a sceptic, but it’s proved successful.

The supposed crackdown on holding at corners and similar restarts, which barely made it out of August. More radical solutions are needed unless teams voluntarily clean up their act, which seems unlikely.

Here are three ideas that could help reduce or end holding at corners.
